Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
250 AM EDT Mon Aug 17 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 250 AM EDT Monday...

No significant changes.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 250 AM EDT Monday...

1. Rounds of scattered showers today, with a few thunderstorms 
possible especially mid afternoon through early evening. 

2. Another weak frontal system will bring shower and 
thunderstorm chances Wednesday, with mostly dry and 
seasonable weather otherwise midweek. 

3. A quiet second half of the week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 250 AM EDT Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Rain overnight/early this morning has proven to be on 
the light side of possible outcomes, with most of the heavier 
showers staying in southern Quebec closer to where a subtle 
trough has been draped. As a result, much of Vermont and 
northern New York has seen little or no rain with only spotty 
showers moving across northern areas. The situation will change 
during the day as the weak frontal system gradually approaches 
and passes through our region. The primary surface trough/wind 
shift line will be oriented from northeast to southwest, and 
showers will tend to organize along it. Poor upper level forcing
and abundant dry air aloft nosing in from the west, evident in 
water vapor satellite imagery, will minimize the potential for 
showers and thunderstorms in most of northern New York. Farther 
east, diurnal heating ahead of the boundary will occur with 
breaks in cloud cover allowing temperatures to rise into the 75 
to 80 range with dew points in the middle 60s. This heat will 
overlap sufficiently deep moisture and instability to support a 
low risk of a thunderstorm in a swath from eastern Essex County 
New York northeastward across much of northeastern Vermont and 
points south. The CAPE and shear balance for thunderstorms with 
a minimal severe threat remains evident in the HRRR/RAP/RRFS 
guidance, particularly in southern Champlain Valley in the 4 to 
6 PM window when mean mixed layer CAPE reaches the 500-800 J/kg 
range with effective shear of about 25 knots (0-6 km shear only 
about 30 knots). Compared to convective guidance 24 hours ago, 
surface based instability has only ticked up very slightly, and 
model output statistics driving the NBM are less bullish than 
the dynamical models for the thunderstorm probabilities today, 
suggesting most showers will not produce thunder. Given the 
relatively small footprint of heavier showers, rainfall amounts 
should be highly variable with localized footprints of upwards 
of 1" while many areas miss out on substantial rain (0.25") 
through this event.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Aside from a low chance of a few terrain driven
showers on Tuesday, the next chance of rain continues to be on
Wednesday. Broad consensus remains that a weak cold front will 
pass through the Northeast during the day and washout somewhere
in our vicinity. This scenario leads to much higher chances of
showers and thunderstorms in northern New York than Vermont,
especially eastern Vermont. The probabilities of thunderstorms
remain low with most guidance rather limited in instability
consistent poor lapse rates amidst a thick overcast along the
frontal zone. Have maintained slight chances of thunder in the
St. Lawrence Valley for the afternoon hours per model consensus
and no mention of thunder elsewhere. Overall, this event remains
unlikely to be impactful. Note timing/location of the front and
associated cloud cover will affect forecast temperatures, which
currently may be a few degrees too high (upper 70s to low 80s) 
in western Vermont and points west if clouds overspread our 
region on the earlier side. Shower chances could linger into
Thursday, although chances are much lower than on Wednesday, per
ensemble guidance; some deterministic guidance suggests at 
least some hit or miss showers will develop in cyclonic flow.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Broad cyclonic flow slowly migrates eastward during the 
second half of the week, bringing near normal temperatures and dry 
conditions through Saturday. Sunday's forecast hasn't fully come 
into focus at this time, but we have potential for a system to bring 
in widespread shower activity throughout the day. A consensus 
forecast will likely emerge over the next few days and we'll be able 
to hone in on the specifics.

&&

.AVIATION /06Z MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Through 06Z Tuesday...Shower activity overnight will be primarily
limited to the vicinity of the international border with ceilings
lowering into MVFR conditions at many locations. The stronger south
/southwest flow should prevent fog formation at most locations, with
possible exceptions for SLK, MPV, and EFK. The winds will be
enhanced with channeled flow through the Champlain Valley, leaving
winds above 20kt at BTV.

Outlook...

Tuesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday: VFR. Likely SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Wednesday Night: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Thursday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Thursday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Friday: VFR. NO SIG WX.

&&

.MARINE...
As of 230 AM EDT Monday...
A Lake Wind Advisory remains in effect for this morning for Lake
Champlain as steady south/southeast winds persist. Observed 
winds overnight have been 20-30kt with gusts as high as 35 knots
over the broad lake and northern waters. Observed significant 
wave heights have averaged in excess of 2 feet in the vicinity 
of Valcour Island, suggesting wave heights of 3-5 ft have been 
occurring nearer to Colchester Point. Winds and waves will begin
to slacken after sunrise, although they will linger in the 15 
to 20 knot range throughout the morning prior to a cold front 
moving through and winds turn northerly.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...None.
NY...None.

&&

$$
